newsitem.title: CHINA: Cambodia's King Sihanouk calls for ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's King Sihanouk calls for ceasefire.

text.p: Cambodian King Sihanouk appealed for an immediate end to fighting in Phnom Penh on Sunday, saying the country's warring prime ministers should hurry to visit him in Beijing to hammer out a solution.
"Please stop fighting right away without any preconditions," Sihanouk said in a statement issued from his residence in Beijing.

Heavy fighting raged in Phnom Penh for a second day on Sunday as forces loyal to Cambodia's First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh battled those supporting his rival, Second Prime Minister Hun Sen.

The situation was grave and both sides should act quickly to avoid the loss of Cambodia's reputation, Sihanouk said in his statement, addressed both to his son Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party and to Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party.
The king called on both prime ministers as well as president of parliament Chea Sim to come to Beijing, where Sihanouk has been receiving medical treatment.

"I request His Excellency Chea Sim, His Highness Prince Ranariddh and His Excellency Hun Sen to please come to see me right away at my residence in Beijing so that we can together solve these most serious problems," he said.

"I beg to request all my children of the FUNCINPEC party, and my children of the Cambodian People's Party, and soldiers and police of both sides, to have pity for the nation and for the population of the country as a whole," he said.
Sihanouk issued his appeal as thousands of people fled Phnom Penh or were loading up possessions to leave.

Ranariddh has accused Hun Sen of launching a coup, but a radio station loyal to the People's Party leader denied the charge, saying if that were so Ranariddh's ministers and officials would have been arrested.
Ranariddh was believed to be in France. The two prime ministers head a fractured coalition government formed amid the threat of civil war after a United Nations-run election in 1993.
As Cambodia's monarch, Sihanouk has little political power but is considered to retain wide popularity in the war-torn Southeast Asian nation.
He has spent extended periods in Beijing since being deposed from power by a U.S.-backed 1970 coup and in recent years has frequently returned to the Chinese capital for medical treatment.
